name: Congenital Bile Acid Synthesis Defect
aliases: Inborn error of bile acid synthesis

clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive inborn errors in which enzymes converting cholesterol to the primary bile acids (cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid) are deficient, so normal bile acids are not produced and hepatotoxic atypical intermediates accumulate.

The commonest form is 3-beta-hydroxy-delta-5-C27-steroid oxidoreductase (HSD3B7) deficiency; delta-4-3-oxosteroid 5-beta-reductase (AKR1D1) deficiency typically presents earlier with more severe neonatal cholestasis and coagulopathy.

The classic biochemical paradox is neonatal or infantile cholestatic jaundice with conspicuously normal or low serum total bile acid levels and a normal or near-normal gamma-glutamyl transferase, unlike most other cholestatic disorders.
Pruritus is characteristically absent or mild despite significant cholestasis, because the retained compounds are atypical bile acid precursors rather than the pruritogenic primary bile acids.
Fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption is prominent, so vitamin K-responsive coagulopathy, rickets, and vitamin E-related neurological signs may dominate the early picture.

Diagnosis rests on urinary bile acid analysis by mass spectrometry (fast atom bombardment or tandem MS), which reveals the specific atypical sulphated and glycosylated intermediates and absent or reduced normal primary bile acids.

Oral primary bile acid replacement (a cholic-acid-based approach) is one of the few genuinely disease-modifying treatments in paediatric cholestasis, suppressing the toxic intermediates and often reversing liver injury if started early.
Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CYP27A1) and the peroxisomal bile acid amidation defects are related but distinct disorders within the wider spectrum of bile acid synthesis and conjugation defects.
reference.pathophysiology: This is a heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive disorders caused by deficiency of one of the enzymes in the multistep hepatic pathway that converts cholesterol into the primary bile acids cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid. The most frequently identified defect involves the HSD3B7 gene encoding 3-beta-hydroxy-delta-5-C27-steroid oxidoreductase, an early microsomal step; other recognised forms involve AKR1D1 (delta-4-3-oxosteroid 5-beta-reductase), CYP7B1 (oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase), CYP27A1 (sterol 27-hydroxylase, giving cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis), and the amidation defects BAAT and SLC27A5. Loss of enzyme activity means the normal primary bile acids that drive bile flow and provide negative feedback on synthesis are not generated, while upstream cholesterol-derived intermediates are shunted into atypical mono-hydroxy and unsaturated oxo-bile acids that are cholestatic and hepatotoxic. The deficiency of normal bile acids in the intestinal lumen impairs micelle formation and hence absorption of dietary fat and the fat-soluble vitamins, while accumulation of the toxic precursors within hepatocytes produces progressive cholestatic liver injury, giant-cell change, and, if untreated, fibrosis and cirrhosis.
additionalDifferentials: Delta-4-3-oxosteroid 5-beta-reductase (AKR1D1) deficiency — sibling subtype with earlier severe neonatal cholestasis
Oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP7B1) deficiency — severe neonatal liver failure form
Bile acid amidation defects (BAAT, SLC27A5) presenting with fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis types 1 and 2 (low gamma-glutamyl transferase cholestasis)
Neonatal sclerosing cholangitis and biliary atresia
Zellweger spectrum and other peroxisomal disorders with abnormal bile acid intermediates
additionalInvestigations: Urinary bile acid profiling by mass spectrometry (fast atom bombardment or tandem MS) to identify the specific atypical intermediates
Serum total bile acid measurement (characteristically normal or low despite cholestasis)
Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (typically normal or low, aiding differentiation)
Liver function tests with conjugated bilirubin and coagulation studies including vitamin K-responsive correction
Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E) and markers of bone mineralisation
Molecular genetic testing of HSD3B7, AKR1D1, CYP7B1, CYP27A1 and related genes
Liver biopsy showing giant-cell hepatitis, cholestasis and variable fibrosis when the diagnosis is unclear
redFlags: Neonatal or infantile cholestatic jaundice with a paradoxically normal serum bile acid level and normal gamma-glutamyl transferase
Vitamin K-responsive coagulopathy or spontaneous haemorrhage in an infant with cholestasis
Rapidly progressive neonatal liver failure suggesting the more severe reductase or hydroxylase subtypes
Progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis or portal hypertension in an infant not receiving bile acid replacement
Failure to thrive with signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency despite adequate feeding
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and oral primary bile acid replacement, most children have suppression of the toxic intermediates, resolution of cholestasis, and normal growth, avoiding transplantation. Untreated or late-diagnosed disease may progress to cirrhosis and end-stage liver failure requiring transplantation.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because serum bile acids are normal or low, which wrongly seems to exclude a cholestatic disorder
Attributing the picture to idiopathic neonatal hepatitis or biliary atresia and proceeding to unnecessary surgery
Assuming absent pruritus rules out significant cholestasis
Failing to send a specialised urinary bile acid mass spectrometry sample, the key diagnostic test
Starting ursodeoxycholic acid alone, which does not suppress endogenous synthesis of the toxic intermediates as primary bile acid replacement does
references: Clinical reference on inborn errors of metabolism
Consensus guidance on bile acid synthesis disorders
management: Give oral primary bile acid replacement with cholic acid to suppress hepatotoxic atypical intermediates, restore bile flow and re-establish feedback on synthesis
Use chenodeoxycholic acid replacement for the CYP27A1 (cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis) form
Supplement the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K to correct malabsorption
Correct vitamin K-responsive coagulopathy and manage rickets and vitamin E-related neurological signs
Monitor liver function, the urinary bile acid profile, growth and bone mineralisation on treatment
Reserve liver transplantation for established cirrhosis or end-stage disease unresponsive to bile acid replacement
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, with paediatric hepatology follow-up
